Source: "Machine Learning & Sentiment Analysis - Annotated Bibliography" (sha12 b0774147a262), read in full from C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\annotations\. The sidecar C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\b0774147a262.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to fold in. The document lists 8 cited works. Only 4 (Birkenmaier and Lechner; Kim et al.; Peng et al.; Ramey et al.) have annotation text. The other 4 (Alkazzi and Okumura; Joo and Steinert-Threlkeld; Taherdoost and Madanchian; Steinert-Threlkeld) are citation-only.

Overarching argument: Paul treats machine learning and NLP applied to public political text (congressional floor speech, public statements, lobbying filings) as a way to produce actor-level attributes (personality traits, policy positions, emotion) that can be placed on nodes of a social-network-analysis graph. The purpose he names is political intelligence: lobbying strategy, industry alignment, and how to pitch policy to a specific member of Congress.

Research questions and gaps Paul states:
1. Conversion step. Birkenmaier and Lechner, Peng et al., and Ramey et al. each say the pipeline does not specify how a model's output becomes a graph node or vector. This is the most repeated gap in the document.
2. Ambiguity. Birkenmaier and Lechner say the method does not separate ambiguous statements.
3. Conflict. Kim et al. do not show inter-industry conflict over a specific bill, which Paul says matters for political intelligence.
4. Temporal lag. Kim et al. are reactive, not predictive, because filing reports lag current positions.
5. Model limits. Peng et al. say long-distance dependency is the main obstacle for most emotion models; stacking reduces but does not remove it.
6. Venue coverage. Ramey et al. offer no pipeline for textual venues beyond their own, and Paul says a framework for contextual or auditory constraints is also needed.

Synthesis: Birkenmaier and Lechner and Ramey et al. both concern personality measurement from speech or text, with Ramey et al. as the older foundation and Birkenmaier and Lechner as the newer, codebook-backed method. Kim et al. and Birkenmaier and Lechner both concern the actor-to-graph link. Peng et al. supplies the model landscape that the other two would run on.

Self-declared gap: Paul says his own technical grounding is not yet sufficient for Peng et al. and plans a second reading after more background.

Path-finding link: Alkazzi and Okumura is the only multi-agent path-finding item. Paul wrote no annotation for it, so any link to Melange path-finding is not in his words.

paul_notes.doc: Paul's annotation document sha12 d963fd8719df is a short reading list on shortest-path and pathfinding methods for social networks, with an emphasis on personality-aware routing. It has nine citations. Only two carry annotation text: Oropeza-Martinez et al. (2024, A* with OCEAN traits) and Rongkuan et al. (2024, improved A* for tactical environments). The other seven are citation-only. No reviewer comment or highlight file exists for this sha (_annots/d963fd8719df.json is absent), so no reviewer comments were available to merge.
doc_level_notes: Overarching argument (Paul's annotations): routing and pathfinding in social networks should reflect how people actually react and choose, not only shortest distance. Trait-aware A* is the lead candidate, and the open problem is parameterizing personality on edges rather than nodes.

Stated gap 1: no application of the psychological A* variant to a congressional setting. Paul treats the pipeline as transferable and the data-collection gap as already partly filled by existing research.
Stated gap 2: edge-parameter methodology for traits (agents are the nodes, traits are agent attributes).
Stated constraint: OCEAN personality reduces 10 personalities to 4 observable ones, which limits how finely traits can be measured.

Stated gap 3 (Rongkuan): the best heuristic-learning and distributed design are demonstrated on physical military terrain, and rely on a local service cache, so transfer to an abstract social network is unproven.

Synthesis across the two annotated papers: both are A* variants. One adjusts the route for human psychology; the other adjusts the heuristic and architecture for instability. Paul's tags (Oropeza: 'Priority - Structure - Basis'; Rongkuan: 'Priority – Structure – Augmentation') suggest Oropeza is the structural base and Rongkuan an augmentation. Paul did not define the tags in the document, so this reading is an interpretation.

Coverage: seven of nine citations (the six pre-Zareie entries plus Zareie) carry no annotation text, so Paul's stance on them is not recorded here. Their cross-references are title-level only and should be read as topical neighbours, not as Paul's connections.

This is an internal status report on the speech-recognition lane that feeds the Big Five personality work in the Moneyball model. It is not a literature annotation. It cites no external published works, so no bibliographic entries are extracted. Its sources are internal Melange files (big5_methods.md, several big5_*_prereg.md files, fec/collect/fetch_hearings_seq.py, b5_audio_verify.py, b5_audio_build.py, b5_speech_quirks.py, an audit folder), and Melange project brain items (D-013, DE-008, DE-009, the anchor-pad constraint).

Overarching argument: the capture pipeline works. Anchor-based capture (a stimulus anchor pad plus manifest offset, and on-screen chyron, and caption text) pins each member's turn exactly (751/751 offsets; padded/unpadded cross-correlation about 1.000 at median lag 20.00s). That yields a ~161-hour, 448-member voice corpus and a 532-of-533-member speech text corpus of about 57.6M words. Transcription (Gemini plus a pinned local Whisper producer) agrees with YouTube captions at 0.945 mean word coverage (n=30 windows), but this is reference-dependent: 0.745 against condensed C-SPAN text, and no human-gold WER exists yet.

Main synthesis: every attempt to validate audio as a Big Five measurement channel missed, was redundant with text, or was confounded. ES held-out r=+0.208 vanished after controls (partial r=-0.029 after gender and party, since pitch encodes speaker sex). E audio-alone r=+0.228 sat inside the permutation noise floor. The N prereg look missed on all four bars (r=-0.0016, n=110), and the channels appear to carry C/E-flavoured signal rather than N. The one partial positive (Pink-E r=+0.284, ES r=+0.298) cannot yield per-trait claims because audio A and ES are halo-inseparable (|r|=0.819). The ruling of record (D-013, 2026-08-25) pivots audio to descriptive, display-only measurement (triggers, speech-habit signatures, agreement/disagreement) with no engine wiring and no trait-validity claims without a fresh locked prereg.

Reliability and venue findings: quirk rates (Spearman-Brown 0.794), pause behavior (0.799 NPR; 0.882 Sunday shows), volume dynamics (0.708) and pitch variability (0.707) clear the 0.70 bar at 5 units. Floor-speech prosody, F0 slopes and vocal strain do not. Filler rates differ roughly 100x between live Washington Journal (~26 per 1k words) and NPR (0.22 per 1k), so raw cross-venue comparisons are invalid.

Stated gaps and open items (all Paul's calls): rebuild hearings_seq.db to fix the 9.7% (65,912) cross-chamber mis-attribution defect, since the code fix of 2026-08-18 is not yet in the database feeding the desk and antagonism scoring; re-adjudicate 33.7% of kept audio clips lacking identifying content; run the 150-clip human-gold annotation packet to get a real WER; and register two speech test suites (test_cspan_identity.py, test_big5_gold_audio_tdd.py) in a runner, since their production guard currently passes vacuously. The document also notes that identity-from-voice alone was tested once (0/7) and acoustic speaker verification was closed (best EER 0.226), so identity must come from anchors and text, with voice used only as a veto.

Research questions implicit in the text: whether audio carries a stable, independent per-member trait signal (answered mostly negative so far), and whether speech habits are reliable enough to describe members (answered yes for a subset of measures, with venue-specific caveats).

works.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
works.summary:
Birkenmaier and Lechner ask whether a politician's *public* personality, meaning the traits they project rather than their intrinsic traits, can be measured from text. They use Brunswik's lens model: observers only ever see cues, and those cues mix true personality with strategic self-presentation. The operational definitions come from the PoliPers framework. Agency is Assertiveness & Will to Take Control. Communion is Empathy & Compassion. Only the positive poles count, and cues are split into strong and weak.

The data are 45,000 German sentences, 15,000 each from Bundestag speeches, broadcast interviews and Facebook posts, covering 46 party leaders from 2017 to 2024. Few-shot prompting of DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4o reaches macro-F1 0.74-0.77. Fine-tuned XLM-R reaches 0.70, bag-of-words SVM 0.55-0.63, and Llama 3-8B about 0.55-0.60. Human coders agree only moderately (alpha 0.70-0.78), and coders label 89-94% of sentences as having no cue. Strong-only definitions work better than strong plus weak. Only GPT-4o and DeepSeek pass the 18-unit functional test.

For external validity, communion share falls from left to right (LINKE 19% down to AfD and FDP about 6%). In the 2024 debate, Trump's cues were 63% agency and Harris's were 59% communion.

For Melange, this paper is the direct method source for `fec/members/agency_communion_llm.py`. That file copies the codebook, the positive-pole rule and the 18-unit test, and it reproduces the left-greater-than-right communion pattern (D .099 vs R .049). But the build departs from the paper in ways that matter:
- It uses a different model family (Claude Sonnet, in English).
- It keeps weak cues in the score.
- It samples only self-referential floor and hearing sentences, 40 per member.
- It has no human-labelled macro-F1 test set.

The paper says nothing to support the next step the system takes: turning projected persona into susceptibility to lobbying pressure. That mapping (.60 z(communion) − .40 z(agency) in the receptivity layer) is a design prior. Its one behavioural test so far (H4, +0.067 on Nokken-Poole drift) is below the threshold. The paper also gently undercuts the Ramey/Mairesse lexical lineage behind the Big Five reader.
works.question: Can computational text analysis validly measure politicians' public personality, operationalized as the agency and communion traits they project in speeches, interviews and social media posts? Which measurement strategy (supervised SVM, fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa, or zero/few-shot prompting of generative LLMs) yields the most valid measure? (Sections 1 and 3.)
works.method: Measurement workflow (Fig. 2, p.6): codebook development and manual coding, then computational classification with three strategies, then validation under the ValiText framework (Birkenmaier, Wagner and Lechner 2024). Labels: agency / communion / none, with a one-sentence rationale per prediction for prompting (p.8). Strategy 1 (supervised): linear SVM on bag-of-words, following Ramey et al. (2019), with fivefold cross-validation and 80/20 splits (p.8). Strategy 2 (semisupervised): fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa base (279M parameters), threefold CV with 80/20 splits (p.8). Strategy 3 (prompting, no training): GPT-4o (proprietary), Llama 3-8B and DeepSeek-V3, each zero-shot and few-shot, with templates tailored to strong-only vs strong+weak datasets (pp.8-9). Dataset variants: strong-only vs weak+strong; balanced vs unbalanced (where "none" is twice as frequent as each trait class) (p.8). Each model run with three random seeds; metric is macro-F1 averaged across runs (pp.9-10). Validation: (a) agreement with the human test set (macro-F1; Krippendorff's alpha for human coders); (b) structural/functional tests on 18 units (6 self-report items from the Lechner et al. inventory, 6 opposing-pole items expected to be "other", 6 unrelated corpus sentences expected to be "other"); (c) sensitivity to partisan variation using party CHES positions and the debate. Results are reported only for DeepSeek-V3 in the partisan section because it was the only model to pass all earlier steps (p.12).

findings.finding: Prompt-based classification with DeepSeek-V3 is the best-performing strategy on the human-labeled test data; GPT-4o is close behind. Macro-F1 is about 0.74-0.77 across the top configurations.
findings.numbers: DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, strong, balanced: 0.77 (SD 0.02); DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, weak+strong, balanced: 0.76 (SD 0.01); GPT-4o few-shot, strong, balanced: 0.76 (SD 0.01); DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.77 (SD 0.01); GPT-4o few-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.74 (SD 0.00); DeepSeek-V3 zero-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.74 (SD 0.01)

findings.finding: Supervised and semisupervised baselines underperform. The SVM is best on strong balanced data; XLM-RoBERTa is best overall among the non-prompting methods. Llama 3-8B is weakest and most variable across runs.
findings.numbers: SVM: F1 0.63 strong balanced (large SD), 0.59 weak+strong balanced, 0.55 and 0.61 on the two unbalanced sets. XLM-RoBERTa: 0.70 strong balanced (best non-prompt result). Llama 3-8B: about 0.60 balanced and 0.55 unbalanced.

findings.finding: No model exceeds macro-F1 0.80. Human agreement is moderate.
findings.location: Sec. 4.1 and Sec. 5, p.9 and p.14; Table 1, p.10
findings.numbers: Krippendorff's alpha for cue presence: .73 strong, .72 weak+strong. Agency alpha .70 (strong) and .71 (weak+strong); communion .78 and .74.

findings.finding: Human coders mostly label sentences as no cue. Among cue sentences, communion is more common than agency.
findings.numbers: 'none' is 94% of strong-cue sentences and 89% of weak+strong sentences. Among cue sentences, communion is about 56% (strong) and 63% (weak+strong); agency about 44% and 38%.

findings.finding: Only GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 (both few-shot) pass the functional tests reliably; DeepSeek-V3 is the only model that classifies all 18 units correctly on weak+strong labels. SVM, XLM-RoBERTa and Llama 3-8B often fail to reach a 50% pass rate.
findings.numbers: 18 test units: 6 self-report items, 6 opposing-pole items, 6 unrelated corpus sentences. Few-shot GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 get all 18 right on strong labels; zero-shot results are described as satisfactory with minor errors.

findings.finding: Party-level communion tracks the left-right positions of parties on both CHES dimensions: a clear negative relation between CHES position and communion share.
findings.numbers: Communion share by party: LINKE 19%, Greens 12%, SPD 10%, CDU 8%, AfD and FDP about 6% each. The text reports regression lines and standard-error bars but no coefficients, N or CIs in the main text.

related.why: The paper takes its agency and communion definitions, its positive-pole rule and its 18 functional test items from the PoliPers framework (Sec 3.2.1.1 p.7; Sec 4.3). Item title confirmed.

The paper critiques Ramey et al. on validation (no human labels, outdated SVR). This is a method critique, not a contradiction of Ramey's findings. Note the year mismatch: the paper's reference list gives 2019, PSRM 7(1), but the item says 2016.
Meta-analysis of Big Five and LIWC links, relevant to the closed-vocabulary baseline the paper critiques. The paper does not cite it, so the link is the analyst's, not the paper's.
The paper cites Azucar, Marengo and Settanni 2018 (PAID 124: 150-159) for the claim that automated personality prediction performs comparably to traditional approaches (Sec 2.5 p.5). Item matches.
Not cited by the paper. It is a general guide to LLMs for political text classification, relevant background for the prompting-versus-fine-tuning result.
Not cited by the paper. It is the source of the Byrne-style choking composite in receptivity_layer.py (line 189), where the communion-to-susceptibility mapping originates, not the paper.
Not cited by the paper. Expert trait ratings of US senators are a possible multi-rater criterion for future persona validation, which the paper does not test.

works.title: Measuring Elite Personality Using Speech
works.summary:
Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh (PSRM 2016) score Big Five traits for every sitting House member from 1996 to 2014. They run each member-year of Congressional Record floor speech through LIWC and MRC features, then through Mairesse et al.'s pre-trained SMOreg models. Scores sit on a 1-7 scale that is relative to the Record. The method adds an optional leave-one-year-out jackknife and 100 sentence-level bootstrap replications per member-year. Above about 5,000 words a year, confidence intervals narrow to about ±0.15. The paper never validates directly against a personality inventory. Its validity evidence is indirect:
- Lifetime trait means relate to Common Space ideology with the expected signs, but explain only R2 = 0.10 (N = 844).
- Emotional Stability predicts whether a member ever answered the NPAT. Predicted response rises from about 30% to about 53% between -2 SD and +2 SD (N = 598).
- Conscientiousness lowers the share of ceremonial bills a member sponsors (-0.39 to -0.58; N = 3,648 member-Congresses, 104th-112th). A positive Majority × C interaction (+0.27 to +0.29) puts most of that effect in the minority party.

This is the template for Melange's lexical Big Five. fec/members/big5_traits.py names the paper and copies its steps. lep_criterion.py runs the Table 3 ceremonial-share test as its paper-exact C criterion. The test came back null for all three C measures: rho between +0.000 and +0.018, n = 440 members, 115th-118th Congresses pooled, at least 8 sponsored bills each. That run did not split majority from minority, the fault line the paper says carries the effect, so the null is UNSTRATIFIED. The paper also gives no grounds for treating the published RKH scores as ground truth. They come from the same Mairesse-LIWC family, which is why the system's convergence against them is inflated by shared method. Finally, the paper's speechwriter defence covers floor speech only. It does not cover the tweets and interviews the system pools in.
works.question: Can Big Five personality traits of US legislators be measured from floor speech text without surveys, and are the resulting estimates valid and substantively useful? Specifically: (a) do text-based estimates parallel known personality-ideology links, (b) do survey nonresponse rates depend on personality, and (c) does Conscientiousness predict the share of symbolic/ceremonial bills proposed, conditional on majority status.
works.method: Pre-trained Mairesse et al. (2007) SMOreg (SVM regression, Weka) applied to LIWC (2001) and MRCPD features, standardized, in corpus mode: (1) process each member-year's speeches through LIWC and MRCPD; (2) apply the standardized SMOreg models; (3) save Big Five estimates per year; (4) optional jackknife (average of all other years) to reduce language tied to same-year actions; (5) uncertainty from 100 sentence-level bootstrap replications per member-year (Lowe and Benoit 2011), 95% CIs. Scores are on a 1-7 scale and relative to the Congressional Record, not comparable to general-population inventories (fn 10). Validity is indirect: (a) OLS of Common Space scores on lifetime trait means with demographics (Table 1); (b) yearly correlations of traits with LIWC features (Fig 4); (c) authorship/speechwriter checks (Pelosi, Boehner, Ron Paul; p.11); (d) logistic regression of ever responding to NPAT on traits and controls (Table 2, Fig 5); (e) binomial logit of ceremonial-bill share with Majority Party x trait interactions and Congress FE in Model 5 (Table 3, Fig 6). Bill classification follows Volden and Wiseman (2014) title keywords.

findings.finding: Text-based Big Five estimates are stable and precise for incumbent House members over time; uncertainty shrinks with word count.
findings.numbers: Median member ~11,000 words/year. Above ~5,000 words, CI width about 0.3 or less (point estimate +/-0.15 on 1-7 scale). Average CI width ~0.35 (+/-0.175).

findings.finding: Congressional floor speech LIWC category usage closely matches the Pennebaker laboratory corpus used to train the model, so the transfer is judged acceptable.
findings.numbers: Correlation ~0.99 on untransformed scale; Kendall tau-B = 0.72 for rank orderings (p<0.001).

findings.finding: Personality estimates show the expected relationships with Common Space ideology; the model explains only a modest share of ideology variance.
findings.numbers: N = 844. Model 1: Openness -0.26***, Conscientiousness 0.26***, Extraversion -0.15***, Agreeableness -0.17**, Emotional Stability 0.20***; R2 = 0.10. Model 4 (with Female and Birth Year): R2 = 0.16, all four expected-sign traits significant (Agreeableness at p<0.05 in Model 4).

findings.finding: Emotional Stability predicts response to the National Political Awareness Test (NPAT), indicating survey-based elite personality measures suffer selection bias.
findings.numbers: N = 598 (622 in Model 1). Emotional Stability: 0.47* (M1), 0.49* (M2), 0.62** (M3), 0.58** (M4, SE 0.28). Moving Emotional Stability from -2 SD to +2 SD raises predicted response probability from about 30% to about 53% (Model 4).

findings.finding: Conscientiousness reduces the share of ceremonial/symbolic bills proposed, and this effect is smaller for majority-party members.
findings.numbers: Conscientiousness: -0.52*** (M1), -0.39*** (M3), -0.53*** (M4), -0.58*** (M5, with Congress FE). Majority Party x Conscientiousness: +0.27** (M4), +0.29*** (M5). Majority Party x Extraversion: -0.33*** (M4). N = 3,648 (M3-M5). Authors: Conscientiousness affects majority members least (p.17-18); minority members must be highly Conscientious to propose substantive bills.

findings.finding: Speechwriter concern is judged a non-issue: estimates stay stable through Speaker changes and across members with and without speechwriters.
findings.numbers: Speechwriters not hired by most members per House disbursement records (qualitative). Pelosi and Boehner estimates stable even though neither was Speaker at the start of the data.

related.why: Birkenmaier's item text (highlight p.5 and p.8) calls Ramey's pretrained SVM outdated and unvalidated against human annotation, and uses it as a baseline. Verified.
Mondak 2010 is cited in Ramey for personality-ideology findings (pp.8-9). The claim that its expert ratings supply legislator ground truth was not checked against the item.
Not cited in the Ramey text, so this link is analyst opinion; the meta-analysis claim was not checked.
Ramey's LIWC base is Pennebaker and King 1999 and LIWC 2001 (refs). Pennebaker 2003 is not cited; the link is looser than stated.
Ramey's Table 3 outcome uses Volden and Wiseman 2014 ceremonial coding (p.16 and refs). Whether Bucchianeri uses the same coding was not checked.
Not cited in the Ramey text; the pressure-mechanism link is analyst opinion and was not checked.
Not cited in the Ramey text; the media-visibility parallel is analyst opinion and was not checked.

works.title: Psychological Aspects of Natural Language Use: Our Words, Our Selves
works.summary:
Pennebaker, Mehl and Niederhoffer (2003) is a narrative review with no new data. It argues that the way people use words, especially function words such as pronouns, articles and negations, works as a stable individual-difference marker. Their reliability evidence is moderate. Successive 2-minute speech segments correlate at r = 0.51 across 21 categories. Four-week test-retest correlations of everyday speech are 0.41 for standard linguistic categories and only 0.24 for psychological-process categories. The link to personality is weak. Big Five self-reports correlate with word use at r = 0.10 to 0.16 in a few hundred students. Neuroticism goes with more negative-emotion words, fewer positive-emotion words and more first-person singular. Depression is tied to "I" specifically, not me, my or mine. Emotion words make up under 5% of all words, so emotion counts are a weak readout of emotional state. Raters who judge a text's emotionality agree with its language more closely than the writers' own self-reports do. The authors also note that word counts ignore context and irony.

For Paul's systems, this is the stated source for the Pennebaker LIWC base in the affective-N slot, and through Pennebaker and King (1999) for the fallback trait weights in the lexical Big Five. As built, both of those direct uses are now dormant or have moved. Since round 7b, the LIWC base in affective N is only a convergent-validity anchor (r = +.24) and is no longer part of the score. The Pennebaker–King weights in big5_traits.py are overridden whenever mairesse_smoreg.json is present, and it is present. The review's main value here is calibration. With word-trait correlations of r = 0.10 to 0.16, a mean held-out r of .350 against RKH is more than this literature supports, which is consistent with the method-shared inflation the system already records. The low reliability of psychological-process categories also makes the system's failed cross-genre transfers unsurprising. The evidence comes from US college students writing spontaneously. It does not cover staff-written press or floor ritual.
works.question: Can natural word use (open-ended speech and writing, read as style rather than content) serve as a reliable individual-difference marker and as a window onto social, situational, psychological and health processes; and which methods of counting words are available and useful (stated at p. 548)?
works.method: Narrative review organized in sections: (1) six word-count and pattern-analysis methods (General Inquirer, TAS/C, Weintraub's verbal analysis, DICTION, LIWC, Biber factor analysis; LSA as a pattern approach), pp. 549-555; (2) psychometric reliability of word use, pp. 555-556; (3) demographic, personality, mood, need-state, self-esteem and psychopathology links, pp. 556-562; (4) situational, social, deception, upheaval and marital links, pp. 562-567; (5) word use and psychological and health change, including LIWC-based writing-intervention analyses and LSA pronoun-shift analyses, pp. 567-570; (6) discussion of which word classes to study and limitations, pp. 570-572. The review does not pool effects statistically and reports most effects as correlations, percentages or qualitative patterns.

findings.finding: Word-use measures show temporal stability. Across 21 language categories in 5-minute talks, successive 2-minute intervals correlated on average at 0.51 (Gleser et al. 1959). Students' everyday conversation was re-sampled four weeks apart with test-retest r of 0.41 for standard linguistic variables and 0.24 for psychological-process variables.
findings.location: Psychometric Properties of Word Use, pp. 555-556
findings.numbers: r = 0.51 (21 categories, 2-min intervals); r = 0.41 standard variables, r = 0.24 psychological processes (EAR, Mehl & Pennebaker 2002a)

findings.finding: Word use is consistent across topic and social context, so it can be treated as an individual-difference measure. Pennebaker & King (1999) found good internal consistency across text types for 36 LIWC dimensions, and word use was stable across home versus public and work versus amusement settings.
findings.location: Psychometric Properties of Word Use, pp. 555-556
findings.numbers: 36 LIWC dimensions; text samples from diaries, essays and abstracts written across days and years

findings.finding: Language changes with age. Older participants used more positive and fewer negative emotion words, fewer first-person singular references, more future tense and fewer past-tense verbs, and more cognitive-complexity words. Both the cross-sectional study and the novelist/poet longitudinal study converged.
findings.numbers: More than 3,000 participants, 45 studies, 21 labs, 3 countries; 60 text dimensions; 10 authors

findings.finding: Gender differences in word use are reported across studies, but the evidence is uneven. Mulac et al. (2001) found relatively unambiguous effects for 16 features; men used more quantity references, judgmental adjectives, directives and I-references, while women used more intensifiers, emotion references, uncertainty verbs, negations and hedges. Tag questions showed no consistent difference. In everyday conversations of 52 students, men used nearly four times as many swear words, and women used more filler words and positive-emotion references.
findings.numbers: More than 30 studies, 16 features; 52 college students (EAR); men about 4x swear words

findings.finding: Big Five self-reports correlate only modestly with word use. Pennebaker & King (1999) reported correlations of 0.10 to 0.16. Neuroticism related to more negative and fewer positive emotion words and more first-person singular; extraversion to positive emotion and social-process words; agreeableness to more positive and fewer negative emotion words.
findings.location: Traditional Personality Measures, The Big Five, p. 559
findings.numbers: r = 0.10 to 0.16 (Pennebaker & King 1999, multiple writing samples from several hundred college students)

findings.finding: Judges' ratings of text emotionality correlated more strongly with language than writers' or speakers' self-reported emotionality did, which raises the question of which personality 'gold standard' to rely on.
findings.numbers: Two studies cited (Pennebaker & Francis 1996; Berry et al. 1997); no coefficients given in the review

related.why: Real item: Koutsoumpis et al. meta-analysis of Big Five and LIWC correlations (31 samples per rel summary). Plausibly updates the 0.10-0.16 figures. Year unresolved: slug and item say 2024, rel summary says 2022 per PDF; not checked here.
Real item: Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh (PSRM 2016) apply LIWC and MRC features with Mairesse SMOreg models to House floor speech. Matches the system lexical Big Five lineage. Relation holds.

Real item but an unpublished revise-and-resubmit draft (2018). It addresses dictionaries failing on specialized vocabulary, not the review limitation about context and irony. Link is loose; keep as complements only.

Real item (2017, German-language Austrian political text; dictionary plus crowd-coded negativity). It pairs a dictionary with crowd judgments but does not test the review judge-versus-self-report finding. Link is loose.
Real item (Birkenmaier and Lechner 2025; agency and communion in politicians public text). Supplies the elite-population validation the student-based review lacks. Confirmed from item summary.
Real item (2019; vocal pitch and emotional intensity of 74,158 House floor speeches). Measures intensity without emotion-word counts, consistent with the review sparsity point.

works.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians (version 0.1)
works.summary:
PoliPers is a working paper (version 0.1, not peer reviewed) that builds a survey inventory of 15 politically relevant personality facets. Examples are Trust & Faith in Others, Compromise & Cooperativeness, Assertiveness & Will to Take Control, Empathy & Compassion, and Integrity & Honesty. Each facet is mapped to the Big Five, HEXACO, VIA, the Agency/Communion "Big Two" and the Aaldering-Vliegenthart leadership traits. The authors test it in four German samples: self-ratings (N=404), ideal-politician ratings (N=589) and crowd ratings of Trump and Merkel (N=211).

Reliability is uneven. Self-rating alphas run from .44 to .87, and Loyalty, Humility and Compromise all fall at or below .51. Assertiveness splits into two factors: the "power-hungry, claims leadership" item loads reversed in ideal ratings, and observer-rating alpha is .40. Observer ratings carry a large evaluative component. Empathy correlates with likeability at r=.70/.76 and Integrity with rated honesty at .70/.80. Rated facets also correlate with the rater's ideological proximity to the target, for example r=.46 between Integrity and proximity for Trump. The paper calls these "predictive validity", but all of them are concurrent associations measured on the same occasion.

The paper matters here because it is the upstream source of the two facet labels in Paul's agency/communion persona codebook (fec/members/agency_communion_llm.py), which feeds the receptivity layer at PERSONA_W 0.30. It does not test how personality affects response to pressure, lobbying, cosponsorship or votes. Its evidence therefore bears on how the persona construct is defined and on rater-bias risks. It gives no support to the susceptibility signs the engine assigns. It also supports two existing design choices: de-identifying text before LLM rating, and modeling halo as a method factor. Transfer is limited by the setting: German raters, two very prominent leaders, and the 2020-21 era.
works.question: How can political personality be assessed with a comprehensive, facet-level, contextualized, psychometrically validated inventory that works for (a) voters' ideal traits for politicians, (b) citizens' perceptions of actual politicians' traits, and (c) perceived self-other similarity between voters and politicians? (p.2, p.11-12)
works.method: Item construction from explicit facet definitions with two disambiguating trait words per item and balanced positive/negative keying (pp.21-22). 5-point agreement scale (Study 2, 3) and 1-5 scale for facet composites (Study 4). Composite facet scores are prorated means of 4-item scales (Dedication & Sacrifice uses 2 items). Factorial validity: principal components analysis of ipsatized items (centered on each respondent's mean to remove acquiescence) with Horn (1965) parallel analysis, 1,000 random draws, run in Stata fapara (pp.24-25, 28, 30). Reliability: Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability omega from a CFA congeneric model (Raykov, 1997), Stata sem/relicoef (pp.25, 28, 30). Convergent validity: correlations of facet composites with BFI-2-XS domain scores and a three-item Machiavellianism scale (Study 2, Table 3); Study 4 correlations with catch-all candidate measures on 11-point scales (likeability feeling thermometer, vote propensity, honesty, competence, charisma, assertiveness, left-right placement and absolute ideological proximity). Group comparisons: Cohen's d for male vs female prompt (Study 3) and Trump vs Merkel means (Study 4), plus sociodemographic means (Table A3). PCA reported with orthogonal varimax rotation for the prototype and candidate composites (Figures A4, A7).

findings.finding: The framework has 15 politically relevant personality facets (e.g., Trust & Faith in Others; Compromise & Cooperativeness; Assertiveness & Will to take control; Dedication & Sacrifice), each mapped to HEXACO, Big Five, VIA, Agency/Communion, and the Aaldering and Vliegenthart (2016) traits.
findings.numbers: 15 facets; 4-item scales plus one 2-item scale (Dedication & Sacrifice)

findings.finding: Self-rated facet reliabilities (Study 2) were moderate to high for most facets but low for several.
findings.numbers: alpha .44-.87; omega .43-.84. Lowest: Loyalty to Principles alpha .44 / omega .46; Humility alpha .46 / omega .43; Compromise alpha .51 / omega .45. Highest: Dedication alpha .87 / omega .84 (2-item scale)

findings.finding: Self-rated facets converge with the expected Big Five domains in the BFI-2-XS (Study 2): trust, compromise and empathy track Agreeableness; passion tracks Extraversion; optimism and composure track Emotional Stability.
findings.numbers: Trust-A r = .50; Empathy-A r = .48; Compromise-A r = .33; Passion-E r = .57; Optimism-ES r = .63; Self-Confidence-ES r = .56; Manners-C r = .59; Creativity-O r = .33. Machiavellianism: Integrity r = -.44, Empathy r = -.44, Humility r = -.37

findings.finding: Intellect & Mental Acuity correlated unexpectedly with BFI-2 Emotional Stability, mostly driven by one depression item.
Essential unidimensionality for most facets in self-ratings, with Creativity & Problem-Solving the clear exception and Loyalty to Principles borderline.
findings.numbers: Horn parallel analysis retained one component for all facets except Creativity; 15 scales judged essentially unidimensional

findings.finding: Ideal-politician prototypes showed almost no dependence on the politician's gender. Only Assertiveness differed, and it was rated more desirable for a female politician.
findings.location: Study 3 results, p.28; Table A5, p.74
findings.numbers: |d| = .00-.19; Assertiveness d = .19, p = .025 (male N = 289, female N = 300)

related.why: Shared authorship (Birkenmaier, Lechner). PoliPers does not cite this 2025 paper; it cites Repke, Birkenmaier & Lechner 2024. The paper title matches the agency and communion text-cue work the codebook ports, but its content was not re-read here.

PoliPers cites the main article (Rice, Remmel & Mondak 2020) for expert ratings of senators, not this appendix. This appendix is the source of the Senate insider and academic gold panel built in build_big5_senate_gold.py. The PoliPers proximity-bias finding concerns citizen raters, not experts.
PoliPers builds its facets hierarchically from the BFI-2 framework (Soto & John 2017) and validates them against the BFI-2-XS (Study 2, Table 3).

PoliPers cites Amsalem, Zoizner, Sheafer, Walgrave & Loewen (2020, Communication Research) for media visibility in its use-case discussion (around pp.37-38). The vault slug year is 2018 but the title matches. PoliPers does not state the direction of personality effects on visibility; the parenthetical in the original summary is not in PoliPers.

works.title: Online Appendix: Personality on the Hill: Expert Evaluations of U.S. Senators' Psychological Traits
works.summary:
This is the online appendix to *Personality on the Hill*, not the article. It has two tables of mean Big Five ratings of U.S. senators. Table A1 has about 129 rows from Senate insiders and APSA Congressional Fellows and feeds the main paper's Tables 2-5. Table A2 has about 126 rows from academics and is used only in the main paper's Table 1. Each row gives a rating count. The front note adds two facts that matter for anyone using the data. First, senators rated by only one coder appear in the tables but are excluded from every analysis in the main paper. Second, partisan composition is lopsided at the extremes. Democrats are 62% of the insiders' highest scorers and 65% of their lowest. In the academic table, 80% of high scores go to Democrats and 80% of low scores to Republicans. The appendix states no scale anchors, aggregation rule or era.

For Paul's system this is not background reading: it is the frozen external gold. `build_big5_senate_gold.py` turns the PDF into `big5_senate_expert_gold.json` (129 insider rows, 125 academic rows), and the trait validators score against it. So the appendix bears directly on how that gold is used:
- **Rating count.** The main validators keep single-coder rows. The paper drops them. Only some side probes stratify or weight by count.
- **Panel averaging.** The multitrait validator averages the two panels into one target, although the authors treat the academic panel as secondary.
- **Party.** Neither primary validator partials out party, while the academic panel's extremes are 80/80 party-sorted. That fits the recorded pattern that O passes only against academics and that lexical O reversed on the party check. That link is a hypothesis and stays UNVERIFIED.
- **Extraction.** The academic count of 125 against roughly 126 text rows, plus a malformed '4..33' cell, suggests the extractor may silently skip one row.
works.question: Not stated in this appendix. It only describes its two supplemental tables.
works.method: Expert coding: multiple raters score each senator on five traits (openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability). Decimal values (e.g., 4.67, 4.17) suggest averaging across raters, but the aggregation rule is not stated. Raters sometimes used 0.50 increments, retained as coded. Observed values range from 1.50 to 7.00; the scale anchors are not stated.

findings.finding: Democrats hold 62% of senators receiving the highest personality scores in the main article's Table 3, and 65% of the lowest-scoring senators.
findings.location: Online appendix p.1, lines 11-14 (refers to main-article Table 3)
findings.numbers: 62% high; 65% low (Democrats)

findings.finding: Using academic ratings (Table A2 in the text, labelled Table A3 in the front note), 80% of the high scores go to Democrats (Angus King counted as a Democrat) and 80% of the low scores go to Republicans.
findings.numbers: 80% high Democrats; 80% low Republicans

related.why: Item exists. Birkenmaier and Lechner 2025 is a text-based agency and communion measure; brain notes give prompting macro-F1 0.74-0.77. Paul highlighting codebook, Krippendorff alpha and macro-F1 is not found in the brain notes, so that part is unverified. Supplies a validation approach, not this appendix's criterion.

Item exists; ext describes Big Five measurement from floor speech text for US legislators, so the complement relation holds. Calling it the template for the lexical Big Five in Melange is not verified here.
Item exists; ext describes Big Five and LIWC relations across 52 categories. Using it as a realistic convergence ceiling for these panels is the analyst's inference, not the paper's claim.
Item exists; ext describes ideal and actual politician personality profiles, which supports the complement relation to observer-rated public-persona tables.

works.title: Feasibility of Big Data Analytics to Assess Personality Based on Voice Analysis
works.summary:
Rubio, Aguado, Toledano and Fernandez-Gallego (Sensors 2024) recorded about 7-minute mock job interviews with Spanish women, nearly all students. They extracted 1,941 OpenSMILE AVEC-2011 acoustic functionals and correlated them with Big Five scores from three sources: NEO-FFI self-report, close-other ratings and zero-acquaintance expert ratings. In Sample 1 (n=78), the best single feature reached r of about 0.30-0.48 per trait. Expert ratings tracked voice most closely (E 0.48, N -0.47). The paper also says N=100, but its two samples add to 122.

The key result is negative: the top features did not replicate in Sample 2 (n=44). The authors suggest a microphone change may explain this. For prediction, the top five features fed a random forest that sorted people into low, medium or high on each trait, scored by leave-one-out. Self-report accuracy was 43-53%, no better than the 50% you get by always guessing "medium". Expert ratings did best, at 53-60%. The paper never says whether the top five features were chosen inside each fold, so even those figures may be optimistic. The Discussion's numbers also contradict the Results (0.38/0.40 vs 0.47/0.48).

For Melange, the paper backs the audio lane's existing verdict rather than reopening it. The lane uses a related toolkit (eGeMAPS v02 from openSMILE), and its audio Neuroticism (N) pilot was a MISS. Audio is display-only, and the engine never reads it. The paper adds two concrete cautions. First, a change of channel (microphone or venue) can wipe out feature-level findings. Second, a sample of one sex hides the sex confound in pitch variability. Melange measured that confound, but the fix is not on the live branch (see flags).
works.question: Three questions stated on p.5 (Introduction, lines 266-286): (1) Are there voice features related to self-reported Big Five scores (externalization)? (2) Are the voice features related to externalization the same as those related to the accuracy of close-other and expert judgments? (3) Can personality dimensions be predicted from voice recorded with ordinary devices in controlled but not restricted speech, so the approach could fit Asynchronous Video Interviews and personnel selection?
works.method: Voice features: the AVEC 2011 emotion feature set extracted with OpenSMILE 2.3, 1941 features (25 energy/spectral LLDs x 42 functionals, 6 voicing LLDs x 32, 25 delta energy/spectral x 23, 6 delta voicing x 19, 10 voiced/unvoiced durations) (p.6, lines 311-323). Analysis 1 (externalization and accuracy): Pearson-type correlation of all 1941 features with each Big Five score from three criteria (self-report, close-other rubric, expert VAS), then reporting the top features per trait in Sample 1 (Table 4). Replication: the top-correlated self-report feature per trait was re-examined in Sample 2 (Section 3.1.6). Analysis 2 (prediction): for each of five traits, the five highest-correlated features were used; scores were binned into low/medium/high at the 25th and 75th percentiles of training data; random forest classifier (scikit-learn, n_estimators = 20, other defaults); leave-one-out with 100 folds (99 train / 1 test). SVM and multiple linear regression were tried but not reported because random forests did better (p.13, lines 1005-1010). Software: Python with Pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn (p.8). The text does not say whether the five features were selected inside each LOO fold or on the full sample; this is a reviewer note, not a stated fact, and it bears on whether the reported accuracies are out-of-sample. The text also does not name the correlation type or any multiple-comparison correction across 1941 features.

findings.finding: Close-other ratings correlate with self-report on all Big Five dimensions except Openness. Expert ratings match self-report only for Conscientiousness and Extraversion.
findings.numbers: Close-other vs self, significant range 0.32 (Neuroticism) to 0.51 (Extraversion). Expert vs self: 'Responsibility' 0.34 and Extraversion 0.31; both significant, the rest not.

findings.finding: Single voice features correlate moderately with personality ratings in Sample 1. The top correlation per trait and criterion is given in Table 4.
findings.numbers: Self: Extraversion 0.47 (mfcc_sma[3]_lpgain), Neuroticism 0.37, Openness 0.36, Agreeableness -0.33, Conscientiousness 0.30. Experts: Extraversion 0.48, Neuroticism -0.47, Conscientiousness 0.44, Openness -0.36, Agreeableness 0.35. Close others: Openness -0.41, Agreeableness -0.41, Neuroticism 0.32, Extraversion 0.40 (text says 0.40 in one sentence and 0.41 in the next), Conscientiousness -0.30.

findings.finding: Expert ratings showed the strongest voice correlates; the authors read this as expert judgments tracking voice cues more than close-other judgments do.
findings.numbers: Largest correlations with acoustic features came from the non-acquainted expert. Expert Extraversion accuracy 60% was the best prediction cell (Table 6).

findings.finding: The feature-level correlations did not replicate across samples. Sample 2 (self-report only) gave different features, although of similar magnitude.
findings.numbers: Sample 2 top features: Neuroticism mfcc_sma[1]_percentile99.0 r=0.52; Extraversion F0final_sma_quartile3 r=0.46 (p=0.002); Openness mfcc_sma[3]_kurtosis r=0.52; Agreeableness mfcc_sma[2]_skewness r=-0.46 (p=0.002); Conscientiousness mfcc_sma_de[7]_kurtosis r=-0.53. Authors say the results 'did not coincide'.

findings.finding: Three-class (low/medium/high) classification from the top-5 voice features gives overall accuracy above the 33% chance rate for most criteria, but not above the 50% majority-class baseline for self-report.
findings.numbers: All-cases accuracy (%): Self N 50, E 46, O 46, A 53, C 43. Expert N 57, E 60, O 57, A 56, C 53. Close others N 54, E 57, O 45, A 52, C 54. Chance 33%; a constant central-class prediction gives 50% because the central band holds 50% of cases (p.14).

findings.finding: Within-class accuracy is highest for medium-trait cases and lower for low and high cases. Some cells are extreme: the Conscientiousness high-trait cell for self-report is 4.1%.
findings.numbers: Medium-trait accuracy ranges 47.4% to 81.1%; examples: close-other Neuroticism medium 76.4%, expert Neuroticism medium 81.1%. Self-report Conscientiousness high 4.1%, Extraversion high 18.2%. Close-other Conscientiousness low 0%, high 64.3%.

related.why: Real item. Paper cites Marrero (ref 21) for voice samples explaining about 10 percent of trait variance (verified at text line 123).
Real item. Melange Salam-2022 sex check (brain line 111) supports the sex-confound complement; Rubio's all-female sample cannot answer that question.

Real item (title confirmed: audio as data for political research, alignment, features, classification). Fit to channel-instability pitfalls is a reasonable reading; the specific claim was not checked.
Real item (title confirmed: vocal pitch and emotional intensity of congressional speech). Supports the emotional-intensity, not trait, framing.
Real item (title confirmed: expert evaluations of senators' traits). Analogous to the zero-acquaintance expert criterion; the paper itself does not mention it.
Real item (title: measuring elite personality using speech). The rel's claim that Ramey works from words rather than acoustics was not verified.
Real item (title confirmed: threats and challenges in personality computing). Its reproducibility framing fits; the specific selection-leakage attribution was not checked.

works.title: The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and Assessing a Hierarchical Model with 15 Facets to Enhance Bandwidth, Fidelity, and Predictive Power
works.summary:
Soto and John build the BFI-2, a 60-item self-report Big Five inventory. It has 15 facets, three per domain, and each facet has four items with equal numbers of true-keyed and false-keyed items. Validation in independent internet (N = 1,000) and student (N = 470) samples gives domain alphas of at least .83 and facet alphas of .66 to .85. Self-peer agreement averages .56 at the domain level and .49 at the facet level (peer n = 184). Convergence with other Big Five instruments runs from .72 (NEO PI-R) to .92 (BFI). Raw-item PCA finds a sixth component, acquiescence. Within-person centering removes it, and the content-balanced facet scales never produce it. Across 20 self- and peer-reported criteria, BFI-2 facets explain more variance than domains (mean R2 .33 vs .27). The authors stress that facet quality matters more than the number of facets.

Nothing in the paper concerns legislators, lobbying or text. It bears on Paul's systems only through measurement mechanics. (1) The LLM item reader (big5_llm.py) says it uses "balanced keying", but the code keys O, C, E and A at 3 true to 1 false. Only ES is balanced. By the paper's acquiescence logic, a rater that tends to mark items +1 would push O, C, E and A up together and inflate their intercorrelation. The system already worries about this kind of halo. (2) The dormant expert-panel instrument is BFI-2-XS, which takes one item per BFI-2 facet. That panel was CANCELED (see flags). (3) The affective-N LLM read sums pessimism, anxiety, depression and volatility, which roughly match the BFI-2 Negative Emotionality facets. In the paper those facets predict different criteria. (4) The self-peer agreement figures give a realistic ceiling for reading convergence between text-based traits and gold ratings. All transfers are indirect: the paper studies general-population self-report, while the system reads politicians' text with LLM and lexical methods. Everything here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: Can a brief Big Five inventory be built with a robust hierarchical structure (three facets per domain), balanced true-keyed and false-keyed content to control acquiescence, and greater bandwidth, fidelity and predictive power than the original 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI), while keeping the BFI's focus, clarity and brevity?
works.method: Rational-empirical scale development in three studies. Study 1: three facets per domain chosen as one factor-pure facet plus two complementary facets (pp. 15-18); marker adjectives correlated against 885 adjectives, 2,552 IPIP items and 44 BFI items to find item content (pp. 18-19); preliminary pool of 110 items (44 original, 19 revised, 47 new) with at least three true-keyed and three false-keyed items per facet (p. 19). Study 2: rational review plus convergent and discriminant correlations with preliminary scales, and balanced keying, to select 60 items (four per facet, 15 facets, 5 domains of 12 items) (pp. 21-22); PCA with varimax rotation on the development sample, which the authors flag as possibly favorably biased (p. 22). Study 3 (independent samples): alpha and retest reliability; self-peer correlations; PCAs of raw and within-person-centered items; five-component varimax solutions for domains and facets with Tucker-type congruence; CFA of five model sets per domain (single domain, single domain plus acquiescence, positive/negative items, three facets, three facets plus acquiescence; acquiescence factor loadings fixed at 1 and uncorrelated with substantive factors); monotrait-heteromethod and heterotrait correlations with other Big Five measures; IRT test information comparisons with the BFI; and regressions predicting 20 self- and peer-reported criteria from BFI domains, post hoc BFI facets, BFI-2 domains and BFI-2 facets, with facets chosen by forward regression (inclusion p < .01, maximum three predictors) (pp. 22-38).

findings.finding: Hierarchical model: 15 facets (three per Big Five domain) selected as one factor-pure plus two complementary facets per domain. Extraversion: Sociability, Assertiveness, Energy Level. Agreeableness: Compassion, Respectfulness, Trust. Conscientiousness: Organization, Productiveness, Responsibility. Negative Emotionality: Anxiety, Depression, Emotional Volatility. Open-Mindedness: Intellectual Curiosity, Creative Imagination, Aesthetic Sensitivity.
findings.location: Study 1, Phase 1, pp. 15-18; Table 1, p. 61; Conclusion of Study 1, p. 20
findings.numbers: 15 facets; 3 per domain; 110-item preliminary pool (44 original, 19 revised, 47 new)

findings.finding: Final BFI-2: 60 items, four per facet, 12 per domain. Reliability in the scale-development sample (Study 2): domain alphas .87 E, .83 A, .88 C, .91 N, .84 O; facet alphas .65-.84, mean .76. First PCA: all 15 facets loaded most strongly on their intended component (primary loadings at least .73, M = .80); all 60 items loaded most strongly on the intended component (at least .41, M = .60).
findings.numbers: 60 items; domain alpha .83-.91; facet alpha .65-.84 (M = .76); facet primary loadings >= .73 (M = .80); item primary loadings >= .41 (M = .60)

findings.finding: Study 3 reliability: all five domain alphas were at least .83 internet and .85 student; eight-week retest of domains was at least .76 (student). Facet alphas ranged .66-.85 in each sample (mean .76 internet, .77 student); facet retest .66-.83 (mean .73).

works.title: The Role of Emotional Stability in Twitter Conversations
works.summary:
Celli and Rossi (EACL 2012) built an unsupervised tagger that labels Twitter users as neurotic, secure or balanced. It borrows published correlations: linguistic cues from Mairesse et al. 2007 (punctuation, emoticons, long words) and follower/following/retweet counts from Quercia et al. 2011. The tagger ran on about 200,000 English posts sampled from the public timeline in December 2011, giving 5,392 ego-networks. Validation is very small:
- 0.625 accuracy against a 0.5 baseline on 8 Personage users.
- Average F1 0.578 against Analyzewords on 18 users. Analyzewords is a LIWC-style proxy that does not measure the Big Five.

The descriptive results:
- Users tend to talk with others who share their trait. Fig. 4 gives no coefficient and no test.
- Neurotic users post and retweet more. Calm users reply slightly more.
- Neurotic subgraphs have longer chains: average path length 1.551 vs 1.334, diameter 6 vs 5. Calm subgraphs have more mutual ties.

There are no inferential tests and no identification strategy.

For Paul's systems this is a weak, era-bound source. Its main use is as a lineage and caution marker for the psychometrics stack:
- big5_traits.py uses the same Mairesse-style closed-vocabulary ES/N weights.
- The affective-N slot is anchored for convergence to LIWC, and Celli's validation has the same method-shared circularity: a LIWC-family tagger scored against a LIWC-family proxy.
- The trait-homophily claim is the only finding that touches a system decision. The system already tested persona homophily on its own corpus and found it UNEARNED (|r| <= 0.015). An uncoefficiented 2011 Twitter frequency count cannot overturn that.

Nothing here bears on susceptibility to pressure, which is what the receptivity layer's N slot assumes. Every bearing below is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: Do users with the same emotional-stability trait (Big Five; neurotic vs secure/calm) interact differently on Twitter? The paper examines homophily in who talks to whom, posting and retweeting rates, and the shape of the resulting networks (Sec. 1, pp. 10-11; Sec. 4, pp. 14-16).
works.method: Unsupervised personality tagger (Sec. 2.3, pp. 11-13). It uses Pearson correlations from Mairesse et al. 2007 (linguistic cues: exclamation/question marks, emoticons, numbers, long words, word repetition) and Quercia et al. 2011 (following, followers, retweets) in Table 2. A 2,000-post random sample sets the feature averages. Each post yields a secure (s), neurotic (n) or balanced (o) model; the user label is the modal model. Descriptive statistics on the ego-networks, the trait-homophily frequency count (Fig. 4), a posting/retweet/reply comparison (Fig. 5), and Gephi network analysis of neurotic vs calm subgraphs with path length and diameter (Figs. 6-7, p. 15). No inferential tests are reported.

findings.finding: Personality tagger accuracy on human-rated Personage data.
findings.numbers: accuracy 0.625 vs majority baseline 0.5; 8 users x 20 sentences; described as in line with state of the art

findings.finding: Agreement with Analyzewords proxy scores on 18 Twitter users.
findings.numbers: neurotic: precision 0.8, recall 0.615, F1 0.695; secure: precision 0.375, recall 0.6, F1 0.462; average P 0.587, R 0.607, F1 0.578

findings.finding: Trait distribution in the English corpus.
findings.numbers: calm 56.1%, neurotic 39.2%, balanced 4.7%

findings.finding: Homophily: users tend to converse with others sharing their trait.
findings.numbers: no coefficients in the text; described as a general tendency

findings.finding: Neurotic users post and retweet more; calm users are slightly more inclined to reply.
findings.numbers: no values in the text layer

findings.finding: Neurotic networks have longer chains; calm networks have more mutual ties.
findings.numbers: average path length neurotic 1.551 vs calm 1.334; network diameter 6 (neurotic) vs 5 (calm)

related.why: Same first author's later review of personality computing. It places this 2012 unsupervised tagger within the field's later threats and validity critiques.
Closed-vocabulary Big Five from text with ES reported and N = -ES, the template big5_traits.py follows. Ramey applies it to legislators, Celli to Twitter users.
Meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five correlations. It gives the effect-size ceiling for the Mairesse-style cues Celli relies on.
Meta-analysis of predicting the Big Five from social media footprints. It benchmarks how weak Celli's 0.625 accuracy and 0.578 F1 are.
Offline Big Five friendship-network selection study. It is a stronger, longitudinal test of the trait homophily that Celli only describes.
Source of the N-under-pressure premise the receptivity layer uses. Celli's N findings concern conversation structure, not pressure response, so the two do not corroborate each other.
LIWC word-category foundations (negemo, first-person singular) behind both Celli's cues and the system's affective-N anchor.
Big Five prediction from Twitter text. It is the regression-based counterpart to Celli's unsupervised Twitter tagger.
